c: Presenter: So this is work that we've published
on recently where we talk about the obstacles
we see to automating alignment. So I'm going to run through that quickly. And
this is work that was done with Marie, with Jacob Pfau, and Geoffrey Irving.
So just before we actually kick off, I think I'll
start with some key takeaways. The first one is
that we don't believe that solving scheming is enough to safely automate alignment research.
The second is that we think we should be concerned about undetected systematic
errors in automated research outputs, and these arise from automating hard-to-supervise fuzzy
tasks. The third is that we believe this
problem is relevant not just down the line,
but it's relevant today to the early stages
of automation, even when humans are writing
the safety cases. We think these errors could be
harder to detect in AI research, and it's possible
that automation could slow alignment progress. And then
finally, we think that the current scalable
oversight protocols that we have are likely to
be insufficient for what we need them to do.
How's that? Awesome.
Cool. Okay, so these are the key takeaways from our
paper. And just to give you a little bit of
an outline of the talk today, I'm going to start
off by presenting what a plan might look like to
try and automate alignment research. I'm going to
talk a little bit about this failure mode
of undetected systematic errors. I'm going to explain
why we think this is worse for automated
research than the human baseline, and then talk
a little bit about solutions and open problems.
There should be a lot of time for questions at
the end, so please interrupt me if you've got
any questions, but if you've got any larger
ones, there should be loads of time. Okay,
so a plan for automated alignment. Well, it might
look something like this. You might want to build
agents that can do empirical alignment work. Confirm that they're not scheming.
Use these agents to build empirical safety cases
or risk reports for each successive generation
of agents and eventually hand over primary responsibility for the research when the agents
are outperforming humans. And so it might look
something like this. Your humans might generate
some research. They might vouch for the safety
of your first-generation agent. And together with
humans, they produce more research. They vouch for the safety of the second-generation agent
and so on. And in this way, you
can bootstrap all the way to alignment of superintelligence.
And over time, these iterations change. We expect
more of the research to be taken up
by agents as time goes on. So an obvious question
is, why is this appealing? Why might we want to
do this? And the reason that we might want to
do this is because it seems that we've reduced
a very difficult problem of directly aligning superintelligence into a much simpler problem
of ensuring that we have a non-scheming research
assistant to help us with alignment research.
What's the goal of an automated alignment program then?
What are we actually trying to do? We think
the goal of an automated alignment program, or
at least the output, is what we're calling an
overall safety assessment. And you can think of
this as an estimate of the probability that the
next-generation agent isn't scheming. And this is sort
of like a generalization of a safety
case. It could be evidenced by a safety case, by
a risk report, by a lot of experiments. It could
even be implicit through staff surveys. And we
want it to be calibrated and also demonstrate
that there's low risk. There are very, very
various ways that this plan could play out. We
could be successful — we could manage to align
our agents — and we could be unsuccessful. And
within successful, we can either know that we've
succeeded or we can not know that we
succeeded. If we're unsuccessful, we could fail and
know that we failed to find an alignment
solution. We could also fail but not realize
it, and fail because our agents are actually
secretly sabotaging our alignment research. And then finally, we could fail but not due
to sabotage, just because there are undetected systematic errors in the research outputs that
are generated by these agents. And this is
the failure mode we're going to talk about today.
Okay, so just to give you a little flavor of
what we think this might look like, I wanted to paint
a little sketch of how automation might look in
the early and later stages of alignment. So the
early stages — well, I don't know if you
saw, but Anthropic published a paper recently called the
Automated Weak-to-Strong Researcher, and this is the sort
of flavor of thing we expect to
happen during the early stages. In that paper,
humans picked an alignment metric — in that
case the performance gap recovered — and agents
optimized against that metric. So in these stages,
we think the agents are going to act
mostly like research assistants, research engineers, research
scientists. They're going to hill-climb on metrics that humans are setting. They'll run experiments,
they'll generate evaluation artifacts. But the humans are still responsible for proposing new
directions, for setting and aligning the metrics for the agents to optimize against,
and for aggregating all the information that they learn and producing overall safety assessments.
And the key distinction here is that the
humans are performing most of the fuzzy tasks. The
agents are performing crisp tasks, but these contain
many judgment calls in the details. So,
for example, an agent might make a particular
decision about how it presents the results
to the human researcher, and that could influence the conclusions that are made.
And as automation progresses, we have this transition where agents perform an
increasing fraction of harder-to-supervise and more load-bearing fuzzy tasks. So they
may generate the actual new research paradigms, generate metrics. They might produce the overall
safety assessments. They might even produce new scalable oversight processes. And the
humans — a nice analogy that we like to use
is that humans are much more like a funding body.
So they allocate resources between different research agendas. They evaluate agent outputs,
and possibly they evaluate outputs through agent-generated scalable oversight protocols.
And there's a key concept that sort of runs through all of this.
That is hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks. So, what's a fuzzy task? Fuzzy tasks are tasks
that lack clear evaluation criteria. So it's very
hard for us to specify whether an output
is good or not, and experts might disagree.
So there are some examples. One might be
identifying objects in images. Another might be judging the quality of writing.
And the third might be drawing conclusions from
a research project. And a key property
of these fuzzy tasks is how difficult they
are for humans to supervise. And there's a spectrum
from easy to supervise to hard to supervise.
On the easier side might be questions like,
does this image contain a bus? On the hard side might be something like,
is this experiment evidence the model is honest?
Easy side, it's relatively easy for a human to
identify what the correct answer is, even if
they can't write down why. On the hard side,
it's much harder for a human to identify whether the output is actually correct.
Okay, so we just outlined briefly what a
plan might look like for automated alignment,
what it might look like going into the
future. And we've talked a little bit
about these hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks. And now I
want to talk a little bit about
failure modes that result from them. Why do we care about hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks?
Well, research is going to contain undetected systematic errors because alignment contains a
lot of these hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks. And this happens whether agents are generating this
research or humans are generating this research. And
there's actually a lot of existing evidence
for this. This is already happening. So this
is from a post by Ryan Greenblatt where he
says that agents are appearing more misaligned when
performing tasks that are harder to verify.
And this mostly contains tasks that are difficult for
humans to spot when the agent might have made
a mistake. And the flavor of mistakes here
is misrepresenting results, not trying hard enough,
even if the task is within the capabilities
of the agent. So hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks lead
to undetected systematic errors. There are two types of hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks that we
think are important for alignment. And they're as
follows. The first is measuring what we care
about. So in alignment, we can't directly measure
the properties of the model that we actually care
about. And that's because we can't safely deploy the
model in a scenario where it could cause harm
and observe whether it takes misaligned actions. So instead, we investigate alignment proxies.
These are things like honesty evaluations, white-box probes, model-organism experiments.
And the difficulty here is making an inference
from your alignment proxy to the actual properties
that you care about. And this inference, this judgment, is a hard-to-supervise fuzzy task
that's pervasive in alignment. The second type of hard-to-supervise fuzzy task that we think
is important is this problem of aggregating correlated information. So when you're trying
to form a safety assessment, you might want to reference thousands of alignment experiments,
and aggregating those thousands of experiments correctly — it's very difficult. It's a difficult
thing for humans to do. To give you
a concrete example here, imagine you have ten research
outputs and all of them tell you that Agent
N+1 isn't scheming. If you treat these as independent
evidence, you might come to the conclusion that
the probability of scheming is relatively low.
But there's uncertainty in the conclusion of each of those research outputs, and this
uncertainty is correlated. And if you mismodel that correlation structure, you can make mistakes
when aggregating those research outputs and come to incorrect conclusions. And critically, this can
happen even if every single one of your
research outputs is correct up to the stated uncertainty.
You might ask, where does this correlation come
from? Well, there are three sources. First is
the agents themselves. They have shared weights, there's shared training data, shared optimization
pressure. The second is humans. There are shared systematic biases between human reviewers. And
the final one is the research process itself. So assumptions, shared methodologies, or conceptual
frameworks. To give you a concrete example here,
imagine that all of your research papers assume
that the persona-selection model is the correct model for understanding agent behavior. There's
correlation through that assumption. And the key difference between human-generated research and
automated research is the agents. So this is
the extra source of correlation. Okay. We know what
automated alignment might look like. We know it contains these hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks.
We know that these fuzzy tasks are going
to result in undetected systematic errors regardless of
who does them. So the big question is,
why is this worse than human-generated research? And
it's worse because we believe that errors are
going to be much harder to spot in automated
research for three reasons. The first reason is optimization pressure. So agent outputs are
going to be optimized to look correct to
human judges. But because alignment contains these
hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks, human feedback doesn't necessarily indicate correctness. And so
the errors are going to be concentrated in
the areas where humans are unlikely to spot them.
The second is alien mistakes. So there's a different cognitive architecture between
humans and agents. And so the type of
mistakes that agents might make could be very different
from the type of mistakes that a human researcher
might make. And if you've got a human reviewer
looking for these mistakes, well, perhaps they're not
looking in the right places. And then finally,
as you move through this process of bootstrapping
to sort of more and more capable models,
you may eventually need superhuman arguments to justify your alignment solutions. And if your
humans can't follow those arguments, well, then they
can't identify where the errors are. So a
particular example about alien mistakes: let's imagine your agent is designing an evaluation,
and it generates a long prompt for the
model being tested. But hidden in this prompt is
an accidental leak that the model is being
evaluated. This is maybe a mistake that a
human researcher is very unlikely to make, and
so reviewers might struggle to find them. Now,
this is a very simple example, and you can imagine
ways of finding this mistake, but it gives you an
idea of this type — or the flavor —
of errors that might be pervasive in automated research.
Okay, and the second reason that we think
it's worse for automated research than it
is for human research is that automated alignment is different to existing human
sciences. So as models are becoming more capable,
we are less and less able to rely
on iteration. It becomes unsafe to deploy the
model and observe whether it takes misaligned
actions. And there's a question here about to
what extent can you rely on iteration or
experiments of weaker models that are perhaps easier to spot whether they've
taken misaligned actions. But the question is about
how far that generalizes, and that itself is
a hard-to-supervise fuzzy inference task. There's also a
much greater volume of research. This poses
problems for aggregating it and forming overall conclusions, and there's increased time pressure.
So I'm just going to run through a
couple of examples here about a few
of the things that we're worried about. So
one of them is, let's imagine that
you're trying to choose between two different alignment techniques. Your first alignment
technique — there's some alignment metric, and maybe that's an agent-generated metric,
and there's some number associated with that. There
are a bunch of papers that have
been written. There's a whole load of compute
that's been spent on that. And then similarly,
for your second technique, there's a different metric.
There are a different number of papers,
and there's a different amount of compute. The
question is, which of these techniques should
you adopt? Well, this is a very hard
judgment problem. It's not obvious to what extent metric
1 and metric 2 capture the things that
you actually care about. It's also not obvious
the extent to which metric 1 and metric 2 relate
to the effort that has been put into optimizing
those metrics. Okay, it looks like technique 1,
there are more papers and more compute,
but does that actually tell you that that
metric has been optimized harder than the other one?
And the second example is if you think back to
the example that we gave about the early stages
of automation, and we spoke about Anthropic's Automated Weak-to-Strong Researcher. In that
paper, the humans were setting a metric, agents were optimizing against the metric.
But eventually, the agents are actually going to
set their own metrics. Setting metrics is a
hard-to-supervise task. They're going to contain errors in
the metrics that they come up with. And
if you optimize against these metrics and produce
more research outputs based on those metrics,
you propagate those errors through the research base. We have these undetected systematic
errors. They're going to be worse in automated
research. What are we going to do about it?
So the obvious question is, how do we train agents to perform these hard-to-supervise
fuzzy tasks well? If we increasingly can't rely
on iteration, we are going to have to
rely on the agents performing these tasks well
themselves. And we see two paths to doing this.
The first is generalization. So this is the idea that
you might not be able to train directly on
a hard-to-supervise task, but perhaps you can find a different training proxy. You
can train on that — that's much easier
— and perhaps that performance generalizes. And the
second is scalable oversight. And that says, well,
there's a hard-to-supervise fuzzy task over here,
but perhaps I can decompose that into easier-to-supervise tasks and
then recombine them in some way to get
some training signal for the hard task.
Let's talk quickly about generalization. So to give
you an example, imagine that what you care
about is designing experiments that reveal whether the model that you're interested in
is honest. And that's hard to train for.
So you think, okay, well, instead let's train on
predicting the outcomes of existing honesty evaluations. And you can see why this might
generalize. It seems like they're getting at the
same thing. And perhaps in learning to predict the
outcomes of the evaluations, your model is going
to learn something about what it is that drives
model behavior. So perhaps it learns something about honesty. But the obvious question is,
well, how do you know? How do we
validate these training proxies if you can't evaluate
performance on the final task? We see two ways that
you might try and do this. The first is
predicting generalization. So, if you're able to, given
a training proxy, predict whether or not it
generalizes to some actual target task, then you
remove the need to evaluate that target task.
The second is maybe you want to try
and improve your ability to actually evaluate
performance on the target task itself. And that's where scalable oversight comes in.
So scalable oversight. Well, we see two problems with current scalable oversight techniques. And
the first one is this question about how
reducible are these hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks. If you
decompose a hard-to-supervise fuzzy research task, it seems likely that the subtasks are
themselves going to be fuzzy. An example here
is: let's imagine that when you're forming an
overall safety assessment that relies on some model-organism experiments, one of your fuzzy
subtasks might be how relevant is this particular
model organism for determining whether or not the
model that you're actually about to deploy is
scheming. So there's this question about how
much can you decompose these fuzzy judgment calls?
Can you decompose them entirely into crisp tasks,
or do they remain in some sense irreducibly
fuzzy? And how fuzzy are those subtasks? Now,
this doesn't mean that your scalable oversight protocol doesn't work
and isn't useful. If your subtasks are easier to evaluate than your main task,
you've still gained something here. The second problem
comes back to this problem of aggregating
correlated evidence. So we're going to use the
example of forming a safety assessment here.
Existing scalable oversight protocols assume that when you're recombining your subtasks,
that recombination process is straightforward. So debate, for example, assumes that you can
take a claim and decompose it into a
deductive argument. But in actual fact, you might expect
your subtasks to be probabilistic and correlated. You
might not know what that correlation structure
is. So this aggregation-recombination process is actually very difficult.
An example: you've got two papers. They both assume the persona-selection model
is correct. But they both use very different experimental setups. It seems obvious these
are correlated in some way. Well, how correlated are they? What number do you
put on that? This is a judgment call. This
is a hard-to-supervise fuzzy task. And this is just
between one single pair of research outputs. You might have significantly more complicated
correlation structures — higher-order correlations between many, many more research outputs. Okay.
So I've given you a lot of problems. I just
want to run through a couple of ideas that we
have about how to follow up on this and
how we might actually work towards solutions. We see
that there are sort of three buckets of research
that you can do. The first is measuring agents'
ability to complete these hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks. Maybe you don't want to just
measure agents. Maybe you can even try and
train them to do these. And this involves gathering
data on hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks. So one example
is perhaps you've got research logs for
some research project that you've done, and these might be intermediate documents, meeting notes,
code from a finished alignment project. You might
want to try and measure the agent's
ability to continue that project against the human baseline,
and you might want to try and pull out,
well, what were the fuzzy judgment calls the agent
had to make? Is another agent able to distinguish
between — let's say, for example, you were doing a
project and at one point an agent proposed some
next step to that project that was then later
corrected by a human. Is another agent able to
distinguish between those two things, between the human-generated solution or the agent-generated
solution? So in this way, maybe we're able to
benchmark or get some handle on to what extent
this actually is a problem. How bad are
agents at these tasks? The second bucket is scalable
oversight. And one particular idea we have here
is: let's imagine you're trying to form these
safety assessments and you've got a bag of
1,000 experiments. Seems very difficult to aggregate
those 1,000 experiments into a conclusion. So you might
say, well, let's make it easier. Let me ask
the agent to pick out five of those experiments, and
maybe that's a much easier process for me to
aggregate. But now you're trading what is a difficult aggregation problem for trust
in the agent's judgment about which of those
experiments you should be paying attention to.
And so maybe something that's better to do is to
train agents to generate a small number of new
research outputs that in some way encapsulate the findings of your original research corpus.
And you can test whether or not that's
a good compactification by getting another agent,
like a weaker agent, to see if they can
predict the outcomes of your original research corpus from
this smaller compactification. This gives you a nice
signal, a nice metric that you can test
whether or not this summarization of information is actually capturing the relevant and important
information that you learned. Why is this useful?
Well, now you've got a small number of experiments
that perhaps a human can go and verify and
look at and check. It might be much easier
for them to actually aggregate to form these
assessments because there's only five of them,
there's only six of them, instead of 1,000.
And finally, generalization. So there's a question
throughout all of this about how far you
can generalize from training on easier tasks.
And the question is, well, we don't know
how far, but perhaps we can run things
like simulated generalization experiments. So perhaps you can test training proxies by
taking research from beyond the knowledge cutoff of a model and testing whether or
not that has — yeah — somewhat like
some ground truth, and testing whether training
agents on training proxies generalizes to them being able to actually solve these
harder-to-supervise fuzzy tasks. There are many more things.
I'm happy to talk about them, but
I'm going to leave it there. And I've got a
lot of time now for questions. So thanks for listening.
Audience: I just want to mention a couple
of ideas that came up during your talk,
just briefly. I'm sure there's lots more that
people can think of, but I was just wondering
about breaking the correlation of failure types between
agents by maybe using a zoo of agents
who've been trained with different subsets of data or different architectural bases,
like non-autoregressive diffusion language models that don't generate text in order but edit random
spots in the text — maybe would give different
biases. I was also wondering about this idea of
maybe we can have agents not need to generalize as much in order to
be useful agents if they're trained on very specific scientific protocols. Like,
this is how you evaluate a generic dataset
and present it such that we can be confident
over a bunch of datasets that it follows this
protocol, and then from there trust that it will
do that on new datasets because it's less
of a generalization if it's just following a protocol.
Presenter: Yeah, great question. So the first question
was about to what extent can we engineer
differences between agents such that their outputs are less correlated,
such that this becomes less of a problem. I think
this is just objectively a good thing to do.
I think that sort of regardless of whether or not you can engineer this,
you still have this correlation problem, right? And it will remain in some sense,
even if you can get them completely independent
in some way, because you still have correlations
through the research process and through your human overseers. And so there's maybe
an open question about to what extent can we extract diversity in agent outputs.
But I still think this leaves — this
leaves your problem of iteration on the table, right?
So science usually works by this iteration process.
Like, I try something, I make a paper,
someone else tries something from that paper, they
realize I was wrong, we correct what I did,
we move forwards. And you might hope that
a sufficiently diverse set of agents can
do something like this. And I think that's a fair
hope. And the worry, though, is that as you become
less and less able to do this sort of iteration
process — because at some point you have to make
a decision about, are we going to deploy this new
model or not? Is it safe or not? — and you
can't throw it out in the world, check
whether or not it makes mistakes, whether it's misaligned,
and then change your research accordingly. This becomes harder and harder and harder to
do. So you're relying more and more on
judgment calls from the human, from other agents about,
you know, is this research actually correct? There's also maybe another question about this
iteration process that happens in normal science. It
doesn't mean that we sort of constantly get
more correct over time. You know, there is this
— the overall credibility of a field is going
to fluctuate over time. And at any one point in
time, you don't know where you are on that. Like,
okay, is my research mostly correct or is
it mostly incorrect? You know that you've
iterated and you've caught some mistakes, but you
don't know that you've fully resolved it.
The second question, from memory, was something like, can you train agents
to do very specific subtasks and follow particular scientific protocols? Maybe that
means that they're less likely to make mistakes. I think,
yes, this is a very good thing to do. You
still have the problem of, okay, if the subtask
that you care about training the agent to do
very well is one of these fuzzy judgment calls
— what's the protocol that we're writing down that
we want the agent to follow? Well, we can't agree
on that ourselves. To a large extent, we rely on
heuristics that scientists have and have developed over
time. And those heuristics are often wrong.
If you look back at the history of science,
there are many examples where we've done things that
have been totally incorrect. So if you look at,
for example, physics — I was a physicist before
this — for a long time, the luminiferous ether was
a thing that was believed to exist, and this
is the medium through which light was believed
to propagate. But eventually Michelson and Morley ran
some experiments, and they demonstrated that that wasn't
true. But for a huge amount of time, that
was scientific consensus. So I think it helps, but I
don't know if it solves all of these problems.
Thank you.
Audience: Thank you for the talk. So I
have two questions that are essentially two different sides
of the same coin. The first one is that
it seems arguable that there's an inherent tension that
for the efforts to make things more monitorable
or supervisable, there may be a tendency for the
scientific communities to converge towards developing agents or problems that may share
more similarities, which arguably in turn might constrict
diversity in one way, which in the
totality may result in, you know, less diverse
opinions in science. Do you think that that could
be a possibility? And the other question is, as scientific agents become more normalized,
would it be possible — or do you
think the emerging risk of agents could be developed
to have risks like scheming or hacking these
metrics in the future, or collusion — that
could be also a factor that we need to
foresee and account for in possibly the near future?
Presenter: Nice. I'll take your second question first
because it's sort of front of mind,
and then we'll come back to the first one. So when I see it,
there are sort of two things that we
can worry about for automating alignment. One is this

I think that remains an important thing that

And so if we're not going to solve this,

Perhaps we need a little bit more time,

But yeah, I think it's true that we should also remain concerned
about scheming and that we should put resources towards trying to resolve that.
Yeah, I think maybe something else is that over
time it's going to become harder and harder for
us to verify whether or not models are
scheming, right? And that's a similar flavor of things,
right? Like, as your models become more capable,
perhaps as they pass the human baseline,
it's going to be harder and harder for us to
find instances of misalignment, just in the same way
that it's going to be harder and harder for us
to find errors in the outputs they produce. So in
some sense, they're similar parts of this problem. But
yes, I agree, I think we shouldn't devote all
our resources to trying to solve this problem.
We should spend them on lots of different problems.
Could you remind me of your first question? Because it's falling away.
Audience: The first one was more about tension.
If people are trying to make the agents more
supervisable in general, that creates like a creativity bottleneck of how science would be,
because human science so far has been relying on different methods,
different diverse opinions to move forward. Could this
be creating a tension, a bottleneck, on that?
Presenter: Yeah, I think this comes down to
— perhaps that's true. But if you're in the
early stages of automation where your humans are
setting agendas and stuff, then I think this is
just a question about how much research diversity
do we have among the research scientists who are
pushing the agents to do these various things?
I think that's a big open question. For example,
to what extent should we rely on theory?
To what extent should we be putting
more resources into conceptual research? To what extent
should we be putting resources into the
more empirical side of research? And how diverse
is the research base? That's a good question. I
think there are reasons to believe that —
I'm not sure whether, from oversight — for example,
maybe I've misunderstood your question. If what we're trying to do is match oversight
to a human overseer, then I think if
we succeed in that, then the diversity that
we have is just the diversity between the
human research scientists. But I do think
that there's perhaps a problem, which is which we spoke
about — let me just bring it up back.
Oh, here, for example — this optimization problem
is a real problem. And this is
where we are putting pressure on these agents to produce things that look good
to us and that are therefore perhaps correlated in the errors that they
share. And those particular errors are also ones that are really hard for us
to spot. So I think that's true and
that's definitely something we should worry about.
Audience: So first, just to check my understanding — we
spent a lot of time on fuzziness, and we care
about fuzziness insofar as it makes tasks harder
to supervise. Is that right? My question is,
what other factors make something harder to supervise?
Like, I can imagine crisp tasks that
are still relatively hard, or fuzzy tasks that
are relatively easy. What else influences that?
Presenter: Yeah, I think the short answer is, I don't know. I guess it's
actually an open question — we also don't even know. So
if I go back to — there was a point where
we spoke about — let me see, Ryan Greenblatt had
this post where he spoke about agents appearing to
be misaligned when they're doing hard tasks. And
maybe one obvious follow-up question from this is,
what hard tasks? And which particular tasks are the agents producing these failures on?
